666.title: Holding your hem
666.hook: leaving praise and blame, I have caught hold of Your hem, sung as the couple takes the scarf (Ramkali ki Var M5, ang 963)
666.howItsDone: At an Anand Karaj, while the bride's father places one end of the groom's palla in her hand, ragis sing Guru Arjan's line about letting go of praise and slander and holding the Lord's hem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahaj, and your line: round four: union. Did you sit with someone and let it be easy? Today we step back to the start of the wedding, to the moment just before the first round. Day six hundred sixty-six.

Before the four rounds begin, there's a small gesture that's easy to miss. The groom has a long scarf over his shoulder. The bride's father stands, takes one end of it, and places it in his daughter's hand. That's all. Nobody makes a speech. But the musicians are singing a line as it happens, and if you know the words, the gesture changes. Because the line isn't about the groom at all.
screen: `A SCARF OVER THE GROOM'S SHOULDER.` → `THE FATHER PLACES ONE END.` → `THE LINE BEING SUNG.`

segments.voice: The scarf is called the palla. The shabad sung while it's placed comes from Guru Arjan's Var in Raag Ramkali, on Ang nine sixty-three. In paraphrase, it says: praise and slander, I have given them all up; I have let everything go. I have seen that all relationships are false, so I have caught hold of Your hem. Read that slowly, and it's startling to sing at a wedding. All relationships are false? On the day two families join? But the singer isn't the bride speaking to the groom. In Gurbani the soul is often the bride and God the Husband. The one whose hem she grabs is the Lord. So the shabad reminds everyone in the room of something tender and a little fierce: the deepest thing to hold on to, the shabad says, isn't another person, even this beloved person. It's the One. One reading draws a lesson for the marriage too: two people who each hold God's hem aren't asking each other to be everything. Then look at what's let go first: praise and slander. Ustat and nindaa. What people say about you, good or bad. A wedding is full of it: the clothes, the food, the gossip about the in-laws. The shabad drops all of it before the first step. The palla itself is just cloth. But held in a bride's hand, with that line in the air, it becomes a picture of a soul taking hold of what won't let go. The couple will walk the four rounds holding it, so neither walks alone.
screen: `THE PALLA: THE WEDDING SCARF.` · `PRAISE AND SLANDER, LET GO.` · `THE HEM IS THE LORD'S.` · `TWO WHO EACH HOLD ON TO GOD.` · then, large: `HOLDING THE HEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a loved one's hand. If someone you love is near, take their hand for a moment, without needing to say why. If no one is near, hold your own hands together, or hold something that belongs to someone you love: a scarf, a ring, a photo. Feel the simple fact of holding on. Then, gently, let go of one thing people say about you, good or bad, that you've been carrying. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you hold. The bell holds the time.
Palla, the end of a scarf, a hem: Guru Arjan's line, sung as the bride takes it, lets go of praise and slander, as the soul catches hold of the Lord's hem.
Your line: holding the hem. Today, when praise or criticism comes your way, let it pass, and notice what you're really holding on to. Day six hundred sixty-six.

667.title: No hot wind touches
667.hook: no hot wind touches the one in the Lord's refuge (Bilaval M5, ang 819)
667.howItsDone: Sikhs often sing or recite taatee vaao na lagaee for protection and comfort: at a birth, before travel, in illness, or at bedtime.

segments.voice: Yesterday, palla, and your line: holding the hem. When praise or criticism came, did you let it pass? Today, a shabad sung when someone loved needs protecting. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

In a Punjabi June, the afternoon wind doesn't cool you. It burns. It comes off the plains like the air from an open oven, and people have a name for it: the loo. Shops pull their shutters, farmers rest under the trees, and mothers keep children indoors until evening. Where that wind blows, shade isn't a nice extra. It's survival. Guru Arjan took that experience and turned it into a line of comfort.
screen: `A PUNJABI JUNE AFTERNOON.` → `THE WIND LIKE AN OVEN.` → `WHAT SHADE MEANS.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Bilaval, on Ang eight nineteen, and it opens: taatee vaao na lagaee, paarbraham sarnaaee. In paraphrase: the hot wind doesn't touch the one who is in the refuge of the Supreme Lord. Then the picture widens. All around me, on four sides, is the Lord's protective circle, so no pain touches me. I met the true Guru, who made this happen; he gave me the medicine of the Lord's Name. Three images hold it together. First, taatee vaao, the hot wind. It stands for whatever scorches: illness, fear, cruelty, grief. Second, sarnaaee, refuge, sanctuary, the place you run to. Third, the circle on four sides, a line drawn around you. It's a picture of a protected space, a boundary that harm can't cross. Then look at the last image, because it quietly answers a hard question. The Guru gives a medicine, aukhadh: the Name. Nobody hands medicine to someone who is perfectly well. So the shabad doesn't picture a life where nothing ever scorches. It pictures someone who has been given what heals, with a line drawn around them while the wind blows. It is sung in hospital rooms, before journeys, when a baby is born, or simply at night. It isn't a charm. It's shade and medicine, held out together.
screen: `TAATEE VAAO: THE HOT WIND.` · `SARNAAEE: THE REFUGE.` · `A CIRCLE ON FOUR SIDES.` · `THE NAME AS MEDICINE.` · then, large: `IN HIS REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find shade and rest. If you can, move to the coolest, quietest spot near you: a shaded window, a chair away from the screen, even just closing your eyes. Sit. Name one hot wind blowing in your life right now. Then picture a circle drawn around you on four sides, and rest inside it for the length of the bell. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or the shabad's opening words, taatee vaao na lagaee. The bell holds the time.
Taatee vaao, the hot wind: Guru Arjan's line says in the refuge of the Supreme Lord, it can't reach the one sheltered there; a protective circle stands on four sides.
Your line: in his refuge. Today, when something scorches, a hard email, bad news, a sharp word, step into the shade for one breath before you answer. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

screen: `DAY 667 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SOME SAY RAM, SOME KHUDA.`

668.title: Some say Ram, some Khuda
668.hook: some call Him Ram, some Khuda, some serve as Gusain, some as Allah (Ramkali M5, ang 885)
668.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this shabad of Guru Arjan in kirtan, and often turn to it at interfaith gatherings as a picture of neighbors who name God differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, taatee vaao, and your line: in his refuge. Did you step into the shade for a breath before answering something sharp? Today, a shabad that walks through a whole street of neighbors. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

Sunrise in an old Punjabi market town. From one direction, the call to prayer. From another, temple bells and someone chanting Ram. A man walks toward the river to bathe; another unrolls a mat to bow. Two neighbors greet each other in different words for the same morning. Guru Arjan lived in streets like that. And in one shabad he simply looked around and listed what he saw, without telling anyone they were wrong. Today: some say Ram.
screen: `AN OLD MARKET TOWN AT SUNRISE.` → `BELLS, A CALL, A CHANT.` → `A SHABAD THAT LISTS WHAT IT SEES.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Ramkali, on Ang eight eighty-five. It opens, in paraphrase: some say Ram, Ram; some say Khuda. Some serve Gusain, some Allah. Ram is a name Hindus use for God. Khuda is the Persian word Muslims in India used. Gusain, a Lord, a master, was used by Hindu devotees; Allah, the Arabic name, by Muslims. Then the refrain: He is the Cause of causes, the Generous One; He showers mercy, the Merciful. Notice the refrain's own words. Kareem and Raheem, generous and merciful, are Arabic names of God, used in Islam, here sung in a Sikh scripture. The shabad keeps going down the street. Some bathe at holy rivers, some go on Hajj. Some do puja, some bow their heads in prayer. Some read the Vedas, some the Kateb, the books Muslims revere. Some wear blue, some white. Some call themselves Hindu, some Muslim. Some ask for one paradise, some for another. It's a portrait of a neighborhood, drawn fairly. Then the last line turns. In paraphrase: Nanak says, whoever recognizes the Lord's hukam, the divine order, knows the Master's secret. The shabad doesn't say the names are all the same thing, or that the practices don't matter. It says that behind every name there's one Lord, and what counts is recognizing His will. It's a shabad for living alongside people who pray differently. In its view, a neighbor's word for God names the same One.
screen: `RAM, KHUDA, GUSAIN, ALLAH.` · `KAREEM AND RAHEEM IN THE REFRAIN.` · `A WHOLE STREET, DRAWN FAIRLY.` · `RECOGNIZE THE HUKAM.` · then, large: `MANY NAMES, ONE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one name you don't use. Sit, and bring to mind a name for God that isn't the one you grew up with, or a name a friend or neighbor uses. Say it silently, once, with respect, the way you'd say a person's name you'd just learned. Then think of someone who prays with that name, and wish them well. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after it, and let the two names sit side by side. The bell holds the time.
Hukam, the divine order: Guru Arjan's shabad says some call the Lord Ram, some Khuda, some Gusain, some Allah, and the one who recognizes it knows His secret.
Your line: many names, one lord. Today, when you hear someone speak of God in words that aren't yours, listen for the One behind them. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

669.title: Blessed is Ram Das
669.hook: the minstrels Satta and Balvand praise the Gurus' light passing on (Ramkali ki Var, ang 968)
669.tomorrow: I never knew what You did
669.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Satta and Balvand's var in kirtan, and quote its phrase about the same light and the same way when speaking of the ten Gurus as one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hukam, and your line: many names, one lord. Did you hear someone name God in other words, and listen for the One? Today, a song by two musicians about one light in many lamps. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

Open the Guru Granth Sahib and you find the Gurus' hymns, and the words of saints the Gurus gathered. But a few pages come from people who were in the room with the Gurus. Among them, tradition says, were two musicians of the Guru's court, Satta and Balvand, who played the rabab and sang. They watched the line of Gurus pass from one to the next, and they wrote about it the way musicians would: in a ballad, a var. Today, one line from it rings out: blessed is Ram Das.
screen: `HYMNS BY GURUS AND SAINTS.` → `AND TWO MUSICIANS IN THE ROOM.` → `A BALLAD, A VAR.`

segments.voice: Their var sits in Raag Ramkali, on Angs nine sixty-six to nine sixty-eight. It's short, and it tells one story: Guru Nanak's light passing to Guru Angad, then to Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan. The line everyone remembers comes early, in a stanza about Guru Angad. In paraphrase: the light is the same, the way is the same; the Master has only changed the body. Jot ohaa, jugat saae. One light, one way. That single phrase holds the Sikh understanding of the ten Gurus: not ten different teachers, but one light passing from lamp to lamp. Then, on Ang nine sixty-eight, the stanza for the fourth Guru opens: dhan dhan Raam Daas gur. In paraphrase: blessed, blessed is Guru Ram Das; the One who made you has also adorned you. And the same stanza names him as one with those before him: you are Nanak, you are Lehna, you are Amar Das. Why does this matter? Because the var is a witness. It isn't a theologian explaining succession. It's two singers, standing close enough to see it, saying: we watched the same light move. Sikhs still sing their var, and the phrase jot ohaa jugat saae is often quoted when people speak of the Gurus as one. The musicians' own names, Satta and Balvand, are in the Guru Granth Sahib forever. The people who carried the tune are kept in the book.
screen: `TWO MINSTRELS, ONE BALLAD.` · `ONE LIGHT, ONE WAY, A NEW BODY.` · `BLESSED, BLESSED IS RAM DAS.` · `WITNESSES, KEPT IN THE BOOK.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT PASSES ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise someone's teacher. Sit and think of a person you admire. Then ask: who taught them? A parent, a coach, a mentor, a grandmother, a book. Picture the light passing from that teacher to the person you admire, and maybe from them to you. Silently say, blessed is the one who taught them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru in thanks for that line of teachers. The bell holds the time.
Jot, light: the musicians Satta and Balvand's ballad about the fourth Guru says the jot is the same, the way is the same, and only the body changes.
Your line: the light passes on. Today, tell someone about a teacher who shaped you, or thank a teacher who shaped someone you love. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

screen: `DAY 669 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I NEVER KNEW WHAT YOU DID.`

670.title: I never knew what You did
670.hook: I didn't recognize what You did; You made me worthy (Mundavani salok M5, ang 1429)
670.howItsDone: This salok of Guru Arjan is read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, at the bhog, just before the Raagmala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jot, and your line: the light passes on. Did you thank a teacher, or tell someone about one? Today, a line about all the help we never noticed. Day six hundred seventy.

Years later, you find out. The neighbor who quietly paid a bill when your family was struggling. The teacher who argued for you in a meeting you never knew happened. The parent who skipped something they wanted so you could have what you needed. You lived through those years thinking you'd managed on your own. Then one day the curtain lifts, and you see the hands that were holding things up the whole time. There's a short salok near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib about exactly that moment. Today: I never knew what You did.
screen: `YEARS LATER, YOU FIND OUT.` → `HELP YOU NEVER SAW.` → `THE CURTAIN LIFTS.`

segments.voice: The salok is by Guru Arjan, on Ang fourteen twenty-nine, right after the Mundavani, the seal he set on the Granth. Its first words are teraa keetaa jaato naahee. In paraphrase: I did not recognize what You did for me; You made me worthy. I am unworthy, with no virtue of my own, and You took pity on me. You had mercy, and I met the true Guru, my friend. Nanak says, if I receive the Name, I live, and my body and mind bloom. Look at the order. First, a confession: I didn't notice. Then the surprise: You made me worthy anyway. The word for worthy is jog. It sounds like yoga, but here it simply means fit, capable, deserving. The worthiness wasn't earned and then rewarded. It was given, and only seen afterward. Where the salok sits matters too. It's among the last words before the Raagmala, the index of raags at the very end. When a family or a gurdwara completes a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, at a bhog, this salok is read near the close. So after more than fourteen hundred pages, the reading ends not with an achievement but with thanks: You did it, and I didn't even know. The same turn can come at the end of any long effort, a degree, a recovery, a hard year: you look back and see the help you missed.
screen: `A SALOK AT THE VERY END.` · `I DIDN'T NOTICE WHAT YOU DID.` · `JOG: MADE FIT, MADE WORTHY.` · `THANKS AT THE CLOSE OF A READING.` · then, large: `YOU MADE ME WORTHY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for help you never noticed. Sit, and let your mind go back to one stretch of your life you think you got through alone. Now look again. Who drove, cooked, covered for you, prayed for you, paid for something? Let one face come. Hold it, and say a silent thank you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for the help you still haven't seen. The bell holds the time.
Jog, fit, worthy: Guru Arjan's salok near the end of the Granth says I didn't recognize what You did for me; unworthy as I was, You made me so.
Your line: you made me worthy. Today, thank one person for help they gave you long ago, even if they've forgotten it. Day six hundred seventy.

671.title: Tell the beloved friend
671.hook: the Tenth Guru's song in the wilderness after Chamkaur: tell the beloved friend the state of his disciples (Dasam, Khayal Patshahi 10)
671.howItsDone: Sikhs sing mitra piaare noo softly in kirtan, and it is often sung in December, during the weeks that recall Chamkaur and the martyrdom of the Guru's sons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jog, and your line: you made me worthy. Did you thank someone for help they'd forgotten giving? Today, a song from the hardest night of the Tenth Guru's life. Day six hundred seventy-one.

A mud fortress at Chamkaur in Punjab, surrounded by a much larger army. Inside, Guru Gobind Singh and a small band of Sikhs. By the end of the fighting, his two elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, are dead, along with many of his companions. At the Sikhs' insistence, the Guru leaves in the dark. Sikh tradition remembers him alone in the forest near Machhiwara, on the cold ground, his clothes torn. And there, it says, he sang. Today: tell the beloved friend.
screen: `A MUD FORTRESS AT CHAMKAUR.` → `TWO SONS FALLEN.` → `ALONE IN THE FOREST, HE SINGS.`

segments.voice: The song is called a khayal, and it's in the Dasam Granth, the collection of writings associated with the Tenth Guru. Much of that collection is in Braj, an old literary language of north India. This song is in Punjabi, simple and close. It begins: mitra piaare noo, haal mureedaan daa kahinaa. In paraphrase: go, tell the beloved Friend the state of His disciples. Without You, soft quilts are like sickness, and living in comfortable houses is like living with snakes. The water jug is like a spike, the cup like a dagger. And then: a straw mat with the Friend is better than grand houses that burn like a furnace. Who's the Friend? God. A disciple, a mureed, is sending word to the Beloved by any messenger who'll go. The striking thing is what's not in it. There's no complaint about the enemy, no counting of losses, no call for revenge. A father who has just lost two sons speaks only of being apart from God, and of preferring the hardest ground with God to every comfort without Him. Historians debate when the khayal was written, and the tradition that places it at Machhiwara is just that, a tradition. But for Sikhs, that setting is how the song is heard. Today it's often sung slowly and softly: a tender song from a Guru whose life was full of steel. Grief, here, isn't hidden. It's sent, as a message, to the Friend.
screen: `A KHAYAL IN PUNJABI.` · `GO, TELL THE BELOVED FRIEND.` · `COMFORT WITHOUT HIM IS SICKNESS.` · `GRIEF SENT AS A MESSAGE.` · then, large: `TELL THE FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: send word to a friend. Sit, and think of someone you haven't told how things really are with you. Picture what you'd say, plainly, without dressing it up. Then, if it feels right, write them a short message after the bell: a few true lines. If you pray, you can tell God the same thing in your own words first, or say Waheguru and let that be the message. The bell holds the time.
Mitra piaare, beloved friend: Guru Gobind Singh's khayal, remembered as sung in the forest after Chamkaur, tells Him His disciples' state; the Friend's straw bed is better than any palace.
Your line: tell the friend. Today, send one honest message to someone who'd want to know how you really are. Day six hundred seventy-one.

672.title: Grant me this
672.hook: deh sivaa bar mohi ihai: grant that I never turn from good deeds and fear no foe (Dasam, Chandi Charitar)
672.howItsDone: Sikhs sing deh sivaa bar mohi ihai at gatherings, in schools and in kirtan, often standing, as a prayer for steadiness in doing good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mitra piaare, and your line: tell the friend. Did you send one honest message? It closes a week that held the hem, rested in His refuge, heard many names for one Lord, watched the light pass on, and gave thanks for unseen help. Today, a short request that Sikhs sing standing tall. Day six hundred seventy-two.
screen: `HOLDING THE HEM · IN HIS REFUGE · MANY NAMES · THE LIGHT PASSES ON · YOU MADE ME WORTHY · TELL THE FRIEND.`

segments.voice: When people ask for something big, it's often comfort: let the test go well, let the scan be clear, let the money come through. Fair enough. This verse asks for something else: the strength not to quit doing what's right, even when it costs. Not an easy road. A steady spine. Not to be spared trouble, but to stay good inside it. Sikhs hold it as the Tenth Guru's, and Sikh children learn to sing it. Today: grant me this.

segments.voice: The verse comes near the end of Chandi Charitar, a long poem in the Dasam Granth. Its first words: deh sivaa bar mohi ihai. In paraphrase: grant me this boon, that I never turn away from good deeds. That when I go to face the enemy, I'm not afraid, and I win with resolve. That I teach my own mind this lesson: to sing Your praises. And when my life's end comes, let me die fighting in the field. Start with the first ask: subh karman te kabhoon na taro. Never turn back from good deeds. That's the center of it. Courage in battle comes after it, and can be read as serving it. Then notice who's being taught: my own mind. The verse doesn't ask God to change other people. It asks for a mind that keeps choosing good. Who is Sivaa, the one being asked? Sikhs read it in different ways. Some hear Sivaa as a name for God's own power, the Timeless One, who is addressed by many names in the Dasam Granth. Others read it within the setting of the poem, which tells of the goddess Chandi's battles, and hear the verse as the poet's request at its close. Scholars discuss it, and the verse is loved either way. Whichever reading, what stays is the shape of the request. It's a prayer for character, not circumstances. The Khalsa ideal of the saint-soldier lives in those four lines: someone gentle enough to sing God's praise, and steady enough never to walk away from what's right.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: commit to one good deed. Sit up straight. Think of one good thing you've been meaning to do and keep putting off: a visit, an apology, a donation, standing up for someone. Picture the moment you'd want to back out, and picture yourself not backing out. Choose it, quietly. If you pray, you can say the verse's first words, deh sivaa bar mohi ihai, or say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Subh karman, good deeds: the Tenth Guru's verse asks, in paraphrase, that I never turn from them, never fear when I face the enemy, and teach my own mind to sing Your praise.
Your line: never turn from good. Today, do the one good deed you chose, even if the moment to back out comes. Day six hundred seventy-two.
